p: He is named with Paul, but the letter is in Paul's voice.
b: Sosthenes is a co-sender, not a co-author: from 1:4 on the letter says "I". He may be the synagogue leader in Corinth whom a crowd beat in front of Gallio's judgment seat (Acts 18:17), who later joined Paul in Ephesus. That is a guess; Sosthenes was a common name. If so, a man who once led the synagogue now stands beside Paul in a letter to the Corinthian church. The Corinthians knew him, and his name tells them that Paul is not writing alone.

p: Paul opens by stating his authority, which some in Corinth doubted.
b: Apostolos means someone sent with the sender's authority. Paul claims the title on the ground of his calling on the road to Damascus, not an appointment by the Twelve, and he has to defend it later in this letter (9:1-2; 15:8-10). The phrase "through the will of God" says the same thing: he did not choose this work. Corinth had teachers who made their own names; Paul begins by saying his place was given.

a: To the church of God that is in Corinth
p: A Roman colony, rich and proud, with a church that met in homes.
b: Greek Corinth was destroyed by Rome in 146 BC and refounded by Julius Caesar as a Roman colony in 44 BC. It sat on the narrow isthmus with two harbors, Lechaeum and Cenchreae, and hosted the Isthmian Games. It was the capital of the province of Achaia, full of freed slaves and traders who had risen by money, which made status a live issue. Paul came from Athens and stayed a year and a half (Acts 18:1-18). The church met in homes; its size is unknown, but the house of Gaius (Romans 16:23) held "the whole church".

t: Already holy, yet told to act holy
p: "Made holy" describes who they are, before it describes how they behave.
b: The verb hagiazo is in a form that means "have been made holy", and "saints" (hagioi) comes from the same root. Paul says this to a church that he will go on to scold for lawsuits, lust and arrogance. In his thinking holiness begins as God's act of setting a people apart, and conduct follows (6:11). The word does not mean they were already sinless. The Old Testament background is Israel, set apart as a holy people (Exodus 19:6).

t: "Their Lord and ours" or "their place and ours"?
p: The last words can attach to the place or to the Lord.
b: The Greek is "in every place, of them and of us". Commentators divide. Many take it with "place": every place where believers meet, theirs in Corinth and ours where Paul and Sosthenes are. Others hear "their Lord and ours", which would tell the Corinthians that the Lord is not theirs alone, and that no church owns him. A third idea is that Paul's letter is meant for all the churches (compare 4:17; 7:17; 14:33). Each reading fits the letter's concern with a church that thought itself special.

a: all who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ
t: Calling on the name of the Lord
p: In the Old Testament this is how people call on YHWH.
b: "To call on the name of the LORD" is an Old Testament phrase for worship and prayer addressed to YHWH (Genesis 4:26; Joel 2:32, which Paul applies to Jesus in Romans 10:13). Here Paul uses it of the Corinthians' calling on "our Lord Jesus Christ". Whether he means that Jesus shares the divine name, or that Jesus is the one through whom and to whom prayer is made, is argued, but the language is the language of worship. The Greek kyrios ("Lord") renders the divine name in the Greek Old Testament. Compare 8:6 and 12:3 ("Jesus is Lord"), and the note on 1:8.

t: The gifts they were proud of
p: Speech and knowledge are the very things the Corinthians boasted about.
b: "Speech" (logos) and "knowledge" (gnosis) are real gifts, and Paul thanks God for them. But they are also what the letter will test: eloquence and wisdom are the stuff of the factions (1:17; 2:1-5), and "knowledge puffs up" in the dispute over idol meat (8:1). Paul's thanks sets the pattern for the letter: he affirms the gift as God's grace, then asks what the Corinthians are doing with it. Note the stress on "in him": they were enriched in Christ, not by themselves.

a: eagerly wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ
p: The word for "revealing" is apokalypsis.
b: Paul puts the Corinthians' future in the return of Christ. This matters later in the letter: some Corinthians seem to think they already share Christ's rule (4:8), and some deny the resurrection of the dead (15:12). The "revealing" is the same word as in the title of the Book of Revelation. Paul keeps the church looking forward, to a day when everything now hidden will be made plain (3:13; 4:5).

a: the day of our Lord Jesus Christ
t: The day of the LORD, now the day of Jesus
p: A Bible phrase for God's coming judgment is applied to Jesus.
b: In the prophets "the day of the LORD" is the day God acts to judge and to save (Amos 5:18-20; Isaiah 2:12). Paul words it as "the day of our Lord Jesus Christ", and elsewhere he writes of the day of the Lord Jesus (5:5). The title that the Greek Bible uses for the LORD, "Lord", is given to Jesus without comment. Larry Hurtado has argued that devotion to Jesus alongside God appears very early in the church; his reading of 8:6 is a main example. See also 3:13 and 4:5, where "the Day" returns.

p: The Greek word is koinonia, often "fellowship".
b: Koinonia means sharing, joint ownership, a business partnership. The Corinthians were called into a shared life with the Son, and by extension with one another. The word returns for the Lord's Supper, a "sharing" in the blood and the body (10:16). A church cut into four parties denies the partnership that the word names.

p: The Greek is a plural "brothers" for the whole group, women included.
b: Adelphoi is masculine in form but names the whole assembly, as in Romans. This Plain English Translation says "brothers" to keep Paul's family language, and the gloss says "brothers and sisters" because the church included women (Chloe, 1:11; Prisca, 16:19). Paul uses the word about forty times in this letter, and almost every time at a turn in the argument: he addresses the Corinthians as family when he rebukes them. Some modern translations use "brothers and sisters"; others keep "brothers" to show the Greek.

a: all of you say the same thing
p: Paul uses the vocabulary of Greek city politics.
b: "Say the same thing", "divisions" (schismata, literally tears in a cloth) and "knit together" (katartizo, to mend or put in order) belong to the language of civic concord. Greek orators urged quarreling cities to "be of one mind" (homonoia). Margaret Mitchell argued that the whole letter is a deliberative speech, a letter urging a divided community to unity, and that the appeal begins here. Not every scholar agrees that the letter has one plan (see the partition theories), but most accept that Paul borrows the civic language of unity.

p: A woman with a household gave Paul the news.
b: Chloe is named as the source, so she was known to Paul and the Corinthians. "Of Chloe" means her household: slaves, freed people or agents who traveled for her business. She may have lived in Corinth or Ephesus; the text does not say. Paul names his source, which was unusual in a letter that rebukes: he tells them who talked. Compare the visit of Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus (16:17) and the letter the Corinthians had written (7:1).

a: Each of you is saying, "I belong to Paul," or "I belong to Apollos," or "I belong to Cephas," or "I belong to Christ."
p: Scholars disagree on how organized the "parties" were.
b: F. C. Baur (1831) read the four slogans as standing for two real groups: a party of Peter, which took in the "Christ party", and a party of Paul, which took in Apollos. Most scholars now doubt that these were organized parties. Paul's own reply in chapters 1-4 deals with one problem, pride in human leaders and their wisdom, not four doctrines. The slogans may be loyalty to a teacher, as students followed rival philosophers and speakers. "I belong to Christ" may be a fourth faction, a proud claim of those who wanted no human teacher, or Paul's own reply. Some scholars read the quarrels as a clash of status, not of theology (see 1:17). The letter does not say whether Peter (Cephas) ever came to Corinth. Some Corinthians knew of him, and Paul speaks of him as a traveling apostle with a wife (9:5), which may mean they had seen him. A later claim that Peter and Paul both taught at Corinth comes from Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, as quoted by Eusebius.

p: A gifted speaker from Alexandria who followed Paul in Corinth.
b: Acts tells of him: "Now a Jew called Apollos, an Alexandrian by birth, arrived in Ephesus. He was a learned speaker and strong in the Scriptures" (Acts 18:24). Priscilla and Aquila taught him more fully, and he went on to Corinth, where he helped the believers (Acts 18:27-28). Paul does not blame him; he refers to him as a fellow worker (3:6-9) and wrote that he urged him to visit again (16:12). The trouble was not Apollos but the Corinthians who ranked teachers.

a: were you baptized into the name of Paul
p: To be baptized into a name was to belong to the person named.
b: "Into the name of" is the language of ownership or allegiance. Believers were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus (Acts 8:16; 19:5; compare 1 Corinthians 6:11, where the washing is "in the name of the Lord Jesus"), while Matthew 28:19 names the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Paul's questions come in a row. The first, "Has Christ been divided?", has no negative word, and some read it as a statement ("Christ is divided!"). The second and third expect "No": Paul was not crucified for them, and they were not baptized into Paul. The point is that the cross and baptism tie them to Christ alone. The Churches differ on what baptism does; see 12:13 and the baptism topic.

p: Paul names the few he baptized himself.
b: Crispus was the leader of the synagogue (Acts 18:8), an early convert, with his household. Gaius is probably the host of Paul and of the whole church (Romans 16:23); Paul wrote Romans from Corinth. Stephanas, with his household, were the first converts in the province of Achaia (16:15). These were people of some means, which fits the picture that the church had a few leading households alongside many poorer members. Paul's point is not that baptism is small but that no one can say he made a following for himself.

p: Does a "household" include infants?
b: Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican churches have used household baptisms (here, Acts 16:15, 33) as support for baptizing infants; Joachim Jeremias argued from the early church's practice that infants were included. Baptist, Pentecostal and Anabaptist churches reply that the texts name only those who heard and believed, and Kurt Aland answered Jeremias on the evidence. Paul says later that the household of Stephanas devoted itself to serving the saints (16:15), which describes adults. The question is not settled by the word "household".

p: Paul rejects a show of eloquence, but he writes a skilled letter.
b: The Greek is "wisdom of speech" (sophia logou). In Corinth, traveling speakers called sophists drew crowds with polished performances, and gained students and money. Bruce Winter argues, in Philo and Paul among the Sophists, that Paul faced that culture. Duane Litfin argues that Paul refuses the conventions of the orator, who aimed to win the audience by skill, and relies only on the message. Stephen Pogoloff ties the quarrels to rhetoric and social status: Corinthians raised their own standing by siding with rhetorical teachers.

p: To Romans, crucifixion was a slave's death, not to be spoken of.
b: Rome crucified slaves, rebels and the lowest criminals. The orator Cicero said the very word "cross" should be far from a Roman citizen's body, thoughts, eyes and ears (Pro Rabirio 16). Martin Hengel collected the ancient evidence to show how shameful it was. To preach a man crucified as the Lord of glory (2:8) was to say that a god's chosen one died the death of a slave. Paul does not soften this; he makes the cross the center of his message (2:2).

p: Both "perishing" and "being saved" are present tense.
b: Paul speaks of two groups on the way: those who are perishing and those who are being saved. Elsewhere he says "we were saved" (Romans 8:24) and "we will be saved" (Romans 5:9-10). Salvation has a past, a present and a future for him, and the Churches stress different parts. Catholic teaching describes justification as forgiveness and also the renewing of the inner person (Catechism 1989), Reformed and Lutheran teaching as a finished verdict with a lifelong growth, and Wesleyan teaching as both new birth and a continuing work. The present tense here is simply a description of the two paths, not a doctrine of the process.

a: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise
p: Paul follows the Greek Isaiah and changes one verb.
b: This quotes Isaiah 29:14, spoken against Judah's leaders who thought themselves wise. The site's Plain English Translation of the Hebrew reads: "The wisdom of its wise men will be lost, and the understanding of its clever men will go into hiding" (Isaiah 29:14). The Septuagint has "I will destroy ... I will hide". Paul keeps "I will destroy" and writes "I will set aside" at the end, a verb used of rejecting a thing as worthless. Some interpreters hold that Paul quotes the passage as a warning that the people who are wise by their own measure are the ones who do not see.

a: Where is the wise person? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age?
p: Greek philosopher, Jewish teacher and city orator: or one figure in three words?
b: The three questions echo Isaiah 33:18: "Where is the clerk? Where is the man with the scales? Where is the one who counted the towers?" (Isaiah 33:18). Here the "wise person" is the Greek sage, the "scribe" the Jewish expert in the Law (or any learned official), and the "debater" (syzetetes, found only here in the New Testament) the public disputer. Some commentators take the three as three kinds of person (Greek sage, Jewish scholar, public speaker); others take all three terms as one class, the learned and clever of any people, named three ways for emphasis. The sense is much the same. Together they stand for every human way of finding God by learning. Paul does not mock learning; he says it did not lead the world to know God (1:21).

a: in the wisdom of God, did not come to know God through its wisdom
t: How the world fails to know God
p: Is Paul denying that people can know God from creation?
b: Paul says the world, "in the wisdom of God", did not know God through its own wisdom. This can mean that God in his wisdom arranged things so that human learning would fail, or that God's wisdom is shown in creation and humans missed it. Compare Romans 1:19-21, where people could know God from what he made but did not honor him. Catholic teaching holds that God can be known with certainty from creation by human reason (Vatican I, Dei Filius; Catechism 36). The older Reformed confessions also teach a real knowledge of God from creation, but one that cannot save and leaves people without excuse (Belgic Confession article 2; Westminster Confession 1.1; Calvin, Institutes 1.3-5). Karl Barth and his followers reject natural theology as a way to God apart from revelation. All of these appeal to Paul's words here and in Romans 1. See the card at Romans 1.

a: Jews ask for signs, and Greeks look for wisdom
p: Two ways to look for God, and neither expected a cross.
b: Jews "ask for signs": a Messiah would come with power. Jesus met the same request (Mark 8:11-12; Matthew 12:38; John 4:48). Josephus tells of men in the first century who led crowds into the desert promising wonders and signs (Antiquities 20.97-98; 20.167-168). "Greeks look for wisdom": the education and philosophy that gave status. Paul speaks in generalities, as the sentence is a pair, and the Corinthian church had both Jews and Gentiles (1:24). He is not saying that every Jew and every Greek acted so.

t: A crucified Messiah and the curse of the law
p: A hanged man was "cursed by God" in the Torah.
b: Deuteronomy says: "a man who is hanged is cursed by God" (Deuteronomy 21:23). Paul himself reads Jesus' crucifixion in that light (Galatians 3:13). A Messiah crucified would be a Messiah cursed. In Justin's Dialogue with Trypho, Trypho objects to just this: he says that whoever is crucified is called accursed in the law (Justin, Dialogue 89). This is the Jewish side of the "stumbling block": not mere pride, but a serious reading of Scripture. See Isaiah 53 for the Christian reply.

a: the power of God and the wisdom of God
p: Paul draws on the Jewish picture of Wisdom as God's agent.
b: In Proverbs 8, Wisdom stands beside God at creation, and Wisdom of Solomon says she is "a vapor rising from God's power" (Wisdom of Solomon 7:25). Paul calls Christ "the power of God and the wisdom of God", and later says all things are "through" him (8:6). Origen and others read this verse to show that the Son is God's own Wisdom (On First Principles 1.2). Arians argued the same verse showed a created power; Nicene writers replied that the Son is God's own. Modern scholars debate how far Paul himself has a Wisdom Christology (James Dunn finds the figure of Wisdom behind Paul's language about Christ).
r: Proverbs 8:22-31; Wisdom of Solomon 7:25-26; 1 Corinthians 8:6; Colossians 1:15-17

p: Not "fleshly sin" but by the ordinary standards of the world.
b: Paul uses "flesh" (sarx) here for the human, earthly way of measuring: education, power and birth. This Plain English Translation keeps "flesh" in every place Paul uses the word so that the reader can see his pattern, and the gloss says "by merely human standards". It is not about the body or about sexual sin. In 3:1-3 the same word describes people who act on human measures even though they are in Christ.

a: Not many of you were wise
p: Mostly ordinary people, with a few of means.
b: "Not many" does not mean "none". Gerd Theissen argued that the church had a few well-off members (Gaius, Crispus, Stephanas) and a majority of ordinary people. Wayne Meeks described many of the people Paul names as high in some ways and low in others, and Justin Meggitt later challenged this picture, arguing that early Christians were socially much alike. This matters for the quarrels: social rank, patronage and boasting were part of life in a Roman colony, and the church brought them in. At the Lord's Supper the rich ate first (11:17-22).

t: God calls what is not into being
p: The phrase recalls God as creator, and is used again in Romans.
b: "The things that are not" are the nobodies of the world. Paul uses language close to his description of God as one "who makes the dead alive and calls the things that are not as though they were" (Romans 4:17). The church of Corinth is God's act of new creation out of nothing. "Bring to nothing" (katargeo) is a key word in these chapters: the rulers (2:6), the stomach and food (6:13), and in the end death (15:26), will all be brought to nothing.

p: Christ is our wisdom, and that wisdom has three results.
b: Christ "became wisdom for us from God", and the three words that follow say what that means: righteousness (being put in the right), holiness (being set apart), redemption (being bought free). They may be three ways of describing wisdom, or three more gifts. Churches read them differently. Reformed and Lutheran writers see "righteousness" as a gift reckoned to the believer in Christ; Catholic teaching joins righteousness and holiness as one gift of inner renewal (Catechism 1989); the Orthodox stress sharing in Christ's life. These are the differences laid out at Romans 3:21-31.

a: Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord
p: Paul gives a short form of Jeremiah's call to boast only in the LORD.
b: Jeremiah warned that the wise, the strong and the rich should not boast in their wisdom, strength or riches. The site's Plain English Translation of Jeremiah reads: "If anyone is to boast, let it be in this alone" (Jeremiah 9:24), and then names knowing the LORD. Paul shortens it, as he does again in 2 Corinthians 10:17, and as Hannah's song is also worded in the Greek (1 Samuel 2:10). Jeremiah's three groups, the wise, the strong and the rich, are the groups Paul has just named (1:26-27). "The Lord" here is God in Jeremiah; Paul's readers would hear Christ (1:30).

a: him as the one who was crucified
p: The Greek form speaks of an act whose result lasts.
b: Estauromenon is a perfect participle: "having been crucified" with a continuing effect, as in the stress that "Christ crucified" (1:23) remains the center after the resurrection. Paul does not mean that he never preached the resurrection (15:3-5). He means that he refused to separate the risen Lord from the cross, in a church that was tempted to prefer glory. See 4:8, where some already thought they reigned.

a: weakness and in fear and in much trembling
p: He came to Corinth after a hard stretch.
b: Acts says Paul came to Corinth from Athens (Acts 18:1), where his speech to the philosophers had met a mixed reception (Acts 17:32-34). Some scholars think he then decided to drop the philosophers' style, but that reading is doubted, since Luke does not say so. Acts reports a night vision in which the Lord told him not to be afraid (Acts 18:9-10). His opponents later said that his bodily presence was weak and his speech contemptible (2 Corinthians 10:10). "Fear and trembling" in the Bible often means awe before God or anxious care (Philippians 2:12).

a: the proof of the Spirit and of power
p: Apodeixis was the term for a logical demonstration.
b: Greek teachers of speech used apodeixis for a proof that settles a matter. Paul uses the word in a surprising way: the proof of his preaching is the Spirit's power in changed lives and in works of power, not an argument. Elsewhere he points to "signs and wonders" (2 Corinthians 12:12; Romans 15:19) and to the Corinthians themselves (9:2). The phrase can mean a proof the Spirit gives, or a proof that shows the Spirit.

p: A word that later groups claimed for an inner circle.
b: Teleioi means complete, full-grown. Paul may be speaking ironically of Corinthians who called themselves "mature" (or "spiritual"), taking their own word and then showing that true maturity is accepting the cross. Others read him as describing all who have the Spirit, or as describing believers who have grown beyond "infants" (3:1). Clement of Alexandria and Origen found here a deeper teaching for advanced Christians. Some second-century groups called themselves "the perfect" in the same way, but no early evidence shows that Paul meant a secret group. See the card at 2:14-15.

p: The pattern comes from Daniel: God hides a secret, then makes it known.
b: In Daniel 2 God "uncovers secrets" and makes them known to the king: "there is a God in heaven who uncovers secrets" (Daniel 2:28). The Greek Daniel calls these secrets mysteria. In Paul a mystery is not a puzzle but a plan hidden in God and now made known in Christ (compare Romans 16:25-26). "Decided beforehand" (proorizo) is the verb Paul uses of God's plan in Romans 8:29-30.

p: Who crucified the Lord of glory?
b: The "rulers" (archontes) may be human authorities: Pilate, Herod, the priests. Chrysostom reads them so (Homily 7). Others hear the spiritual powers behind human rule: Origen takes them as demonic powers (On First Principles 3.2), and Oscar Cullmann argued that both are meant. Paul's phrase "who are coming to nothing" (2:6) and the Jewish idea of powers over the nations favor the second view; the fact that they "crucified" fits the first. Both are common among interpreters.

t: A title of God applied to Jesus
p: Psalm 24 and 1 Enoch use the same title for God.
b: Psalm 24 asks, "who is this King of glory?" (Psalm 24:7-10). In 1 Enoch, which the Ethiopian church counts as Scripture and others do not, God is called "the Lord of glory" (1 Enoch 22:14; 25:3). Paul puts the title on Jesus and says he was crucified. The paradox is that the Lord of glory was crucified.

a: What no eye has seen and no ear has heard
t: Where does this quotation come from?
p: No single Old Testament verse matches it.
b: Paul says "it is written", but the words are a blend. Isaiah 64:4 is close in sense: "no eye has seen a God besides you, one who acts for those who wait for him" (Isaiah 64:4). Isaiah 65:16-17 speaks of what "will not come up upon the heart" in the Greek. Origen attributed the words to a writing connected with Elijah (now called the Apocalypse of Elijah), and Jerome held that Paul probably did not cite that writing. A similar saying appears in 1 Clement 34, 2 Clement 11 and the Gospel of Thomas 17; whether these depend on Paul or on a common source is debated.
r: Isaiah 64:4; Isaiah 65:16-17; Isaiah 52:15; 1 Clement 34:8; Gospel of Thomas 17

t: The Spirit and the depths of God
p: Church fathers used this to show that the Spirit is God.
b: Paul's argument is that only one who knows God's inner life can reveal it, and the Spirit does (2:11). Basil of Caesarea (On the Holy Spirit 16) used 2:10-11 to argue that the Spirit is not a creature: the Spirit knows "the deep things of God", while a creature receives the showing of such things through the Spirit. Paul's own interest is revelation, not the doctrine of the Trinity that came later, but the fathers drew on what he wrote. The Plain English Translation also leaves out the small joining word at the start of 2:10 ("for" in the SBL text, "but" in NA28); see the variant note.

a: putting spiritual things into spiritual words
t: Three ways to read the last clause
p: Pneumatikois pneumatika synkrinontes can be read in three ways.
b: Synkrino means to compare, to combine or to interpret. And pneumatikois can be neuter ("spiritual words") or masculine ("spiritual people"). The readings are: (1) putting spiritual things into spiritual words (this Plain English Translation); (2) explaining spiritual things to spiritual people; (3) comparing spiritual things with spiritual things, which was the old view that Scripture explains Scripture. All three agree that the Spirit is the source of what Paul says and of the hearing of it.

p: Literally "soul-ish": a person with only the life of the soul.
b: Psychikos comes from psyche, the life-breath or soul. The man "made a living psyche" in Genesis 2:7 (in Greek) is what Paul means by "natural" (15:44-46). It is not a bad word in itself; it names an ordinary human being without the Spirit. English versions say "natural", "unspiritual", "without the Spirit" and "worldly". Jude 19 uses the word of people who have "not the Spirit". Paul does not say that such a person is stupid, only that these things are judged by the Spirit.

a: who has come to know the Lord's mind, so as to instruct him?
t: Isaiah 40:13 and the mind of Christ
p: In Isaiah this is God's Spirit; in Paul it becomes the Lord's mind.
b: Isaiah 40:13 in the site's Plain English Translation: "Who has taken the measure of the LORD's Spirit? What adviser of his has taught him anything?" (Isaiah 40:13). The Greek Bible has "mind" where the Hebrew has "Spirit". Paul quotes the same line in Romans 11:34 ("For who has come to know the Lord's mind? Or who has been his adviser?"). Then he says "we have the mind of Christ", which assumes the "Lord" of Isaiah can be named Christ. The claim is not that Christians know everything but that they share Christ's way of thinking, which is the opposite of boasting.

p: A teacher's image for beginners, used with some sting.
b: Nepios is a baby who cannot yet speak (the Latin infans means "without speech"). Teachers of the day used milk and solid food for beginners' lessons and advanced ones; Hebrews 5:12-14 and 1 Peter 2:2 use the picture too. Here it is a rebuke: the Corinthians boasted of wisdom, yet Paul says their quarrels show they are still babies. In the Greek of this verse the word "flesh" is built into "made of flesh" (sarkinos); the variant entry treats the difference from "fleshly" (sarkikos).

p: The same phrase as "according to the flesh" in the sense of merely human.
b: Kata anthropon peripateo is "walking according to man". "Walking" is the Jewish word for a whole way of life (Hebrew halakh, which gives halakhah). The Corinthians' jealousy and strife show that they live by the standards of the world, not by the Spirit. Paul says the same in 3:4: "are you not merely human?". Churches that act as human clubs have stopped acting as the temple of the Spirit (3:16).

a: Servants through whom you came to believe
p: Diakonoi are people who wait on others.
b: Diakonos means a servant who does work for another. It is Paul's word for himself and Apollos, and in Romans 16:1 for Phoebe. Paul does not say "deacon" in the later church sense. John N. Collins argued that the word stresses being an agent sent on a task, not humble service. Either way, the point is the same: the teachers are less important than the God they serve. Their task was given by the Lord "to each one".

a: I planted, Apollos watered, but God made it grow
p: Farm and building images for God's work with his people.
b: God told Jeremiah he was put in charge "to pull up and pull down, to destroy and demolish, to build and to plant" (Jeremiah 1:10). Israel is God's vineyard or planting in the prophets (Isaiah 5:1-7). Paul's two images, field (3:6-9) and building (3:10-17), belong to this pattern: God owns both. A plant grows only because God gives growth, and no gardener should claim the credit.

p: "God's" could mean working with God, or working together as God's people.
b: Theou synergoi can be "co-workers with God" or "co-workers who belong to God". The second is the more natural reading here: Paul and Apollos are fellow workers with each other, and both belong to God, who owns the field and the building. Some Churches use the first reading for the idea that human beings cooperate with God in salvation (Catholic and Orthodox teaching on cooperation with grace); Reformed writers stress that God alone gives growth (3:7). The verse is about the work of ministry, not about the way a person is saved.

p: Not an architect with plans on paper, but the head builder.
b: Architekton is the chief builder who lays the foundation and directs the work. Paul sees his job as the first one, to establish the church (Romans 15:20 says he avoids building on another's foundation). Others, such as Apollos, build on it. Paul does not say he is the only builder; he warns each builder to take care. The Greek word "wise" is used with irony in a chapter that has just undone human wisdom: Paul's wisdom is that he laid the foundation, which is Christ.

t: The foundation: Christ, or Peter, or the apostles?
p: Churches connect this verse with Matthew 16:18 and Ephesians 2:20.
b: Paul says no one can lay any foundation but Christ. Ephesians 2:20 says the church is built "on the apostles and prophets as the foundation, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone". In Matthew Jesus says, "you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church" (Matthew 16:18). Protestant writers often cite 3:11 to say Christ alone is the foundation. Catholic teaching replies that the Church is built on Christ through Peter and the apostles, whom he appointed (Catechism 552-553). These readings do not need to contradict 3:11.

a: gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay or straw
t: Materials that last, materials that burn
p: Two sets of three: what fire cannot harm and what it destroys.
b: Gold, silver and precious stones were used in Solomon's temple and on the high priest's breastpiece; wood, hay and straw are the cheap building materials of a house. The only difference that matters here is what fire does to them. Paul does not say what each stands for. Readers have taken them as kinds of teaching (Calvin, commentary on 3:12), kinds of converts, or kinds of works (Chrysostom takes them as a person's actions, Homily 9). The context (the Corinthians' preference for human wisdom) points to the quality of teaching and the quality of the church built by it.

a: the Day will make it clear
t: The Day and the fire of testing
p: In the Bible, fire tests metal and shows its quality.
b: "The Day" is the day of Christ (1:8; 4:5). In the prophets fire is a refiner's tool: God "refines" his people as silver is refined (Malachi 3:2-3; Zechariah 13:9; Isaiah 1:25). The fire here does not first punish; it tests (dokimazo), as a fire shows gold from straw. Paul leaves open whether this is literal fire or a picture of God's searching judgment. The fire falls on the works, not on the person (3:15).

t: A reward, and what it means
p: Paul separates reward from salvation.
b: A misthos is wages or a reward, which Paul uses in 3:8 and 9:17-18. Here it is clearly not salvation itself, since the builder whose work burns is still saved (3:15). Churches differ on how to speak of reward: Catholic teaching says eternal life is both a grace and a reward promised to good works done by grace (Catechism 2006-2011); Reformed teaching says that God, looking on believers' works in his Son, is pleased to accept and reward what is sincere (Westminster Confession 16). Both traditions stress that no one earns salvation by building well.

p: Zemioo means to be fined or lose something.
b: The Greek verb (zemiothesetai; the Plain English Translation says "forfeit it") is used of losing property (Philippians 3:8) or of suffering damage (Matthew 16:26). What is lost here is the work, and so the reward (3:14), not the person's salvation. Some readers have heard it as a loss of the work's whole fruit: the converts he won but built badly. Either way the verse says that failure in ministry is not the same as failure of faith.

a: like one who comes through fire
p: The most disputed sentence in the chapter.
b: Houtos de hos dia pyros is "yet so, as through fire", a picture. It is like someone running out of a burning house, saved with nothing. The prophets use a similar picture: Israel was "a piece of firewood snatched from the blaze" (Amos 4:11), and Joshua the high priest is "a piece of firewood snatched from the fire" (Zechariah 3:2). Whether the verse also teaches a purifying fire after death is the question of purgatory. The Catholic Catechism says the Church speaks of purgatory "especially at the Councils of Florence and Trent" and appeals to Scripture and tradition (Catechism 1030-1032). Others (Calvin, who reads the passage as the testing of teachers' doctrine; the Thirty-Nine Articles; the Smalcald Articles) deny that the verse teaches it. See the card, and the deep dive on 3:10-17 in the chapter page.

p: The Corinthians together are the building where God lives.
b: "You" is plural, and "temple" is naos, the inner house of the god, where God's presence lived, not the whole temple area (that is hieron). Elsewhere in the New Testament on this site (Matthew, Mark, Luke and Acts) naos is usually rendered "sanctuary" to keep it apart from hieron. Here the Plain English Translation says "temple" because Paul is using the picture of the believers as the place where God lives, and "temple" is the English word that carries that picture. The same choice is made for naos in Paul's other uses (6:19; 2 Corinthians 6:16; Ephesians 2:21). The church, not each single believer, is the place where God dwells here; in 6:19 Paul uses the singular, and the "body" of each believer is a temple. God promised to live among his people (Exodus 25:8; Ezekiel 37:26-28).

p: Phtheiro means to destroy, corrupt or spoil.
b: Paul repeats the word: whoever phtheirei the temple, God will phtheirei him. "Ruin" keeps the echo. The warning is against those who tear apart the church by building on human wisdom and splitting it into camps, not at an ordinary struggling member. Chrysostom takes it as aimed at the church member whose sexual sin Paul deals with in chapter 5 (Homily 9). The sentence is a strong one and Paul gives the reason: the temple is holy, and "you" (all of you) are it.

a: He catches the wise in their cunning
p: Paul quotes one of Job's friends.
b: This is Job 5:13, from the first speech of Eliphaz. The site's Plain English Translation of Job reads: "He snares the wise in their own cunning" (Job 5:13). Paul's Greek is not the Septuagint's (which has "prudence"), and is nearer to the Hebrew. Eliphaz is one of the friends whom God says later "have not spoken rightly" about him (Job 42:7). Interpreters note that a true saying can come from a speaker who is wrong about the case; Paul takes the proverb as true on its own.

a: The Lord knows that the reasonings of the wise are futile
p: Paul changes "human beings" to "the wise".
b: In the Hebrew and the Greek Psalm, God knows the thoughts of human beings (the site's Plain English Translation: "The LORD knows human thinking", Psalm 94:11). Paul writes "of the wise" in place of "of men", to fit his argument. He also uses "futile" (mataios), the root of the word for "futility" in Romans 8:20. A Jewish reader would not hear a contrast between Jew and Gentile here but between God's knowledge and any human mind.

t: Stoics said the same of the wise
p: Paul takes a philosophers' boast and turns it.
b: The Stoic teaching was that "all things belong to the wise person" (Seneca, On Benefits 7.3-4; also Diogenes Laertius 7.125). The Corinthians who thought themselves wise may have used this phrase. Paul agrees that everything is theirs, but the ground is different: they belong to Christ, and Christ to God (3:23). The list "Paul or Apollos or Cephas" ends their rivalry: all the teachers belong to the church, not the church to its teachers. The pronouns run in a chain that later became important in debates over the Son and the Father (see 15:28).

p: A steward was a household slave in charge of the master's goods.
b: Oikonomos is a manager, often a slave or freed slave, who ran a household's affairs (Luke 12:42; Romans 16:23 uses the word for Erastus, "the city treasurer"). Paul names himself and Apollos "assistants" (hyperetai, literally under-rowers) and stewards. "Mysteries" are the plans of God now revealed (2:7). The Latin Bible translated mysterion as sacramentum in some places (Ephesians 1:9; 3:3; 5:32; Colossians 1:27), though here the Vulgate has mysteriorum, "of the mysteries". Many Catholic and Orthodox writers have read the phrase as including the sacraments, while Protestant writers have stressed the preaching of the gospel. Both readings agree that the stewards own nothing.

p: The Greek says "a human day", meaning a court date.
b: Anthropine hemera is literally "a human day", a day on which a human court sits. It is set against "the Day" of the Lord (3:13). The verb "examine" (anakrino) is the word for a formal hearing, used of a judge's inquiry (Acts 4:9; 12:19). Paul uses it for what the Corinthians do to their teachers, ranking them, and says he does not even do it to himself. Only the Lord's examination counts.

a: I am not justified by that
p: Not Paul's usual use of the word.
b: Dedikaiomai is "I have been declared in the right". In Romans the word is mostly about God's verdict that begins the life of faith (Romans 3:24; 5:1). Here it is about the final verdict: a clear conscience does not prove that God will call Paul's work right. It is a reminder that "justify" in Paul can refer both to the beginning of faith and to the last judgment (Romans 2:13). The one who examines is the Lord, who has not yet spoken.

a: Then praise will come to each person from God
p: A day when hidden motives are exposed and praised.
b: Paul looks to a day when the hidden things of darkness and the motives of hearts are made plain. The result for the faithful is praise from God. The picture agrees with 3:13-15 and with 2 Corinthians 5:10 ("the judgment seat of Christ"). Churches describe the judgment in their own terms. Catholic teaching speaks of a particular judgment at death (Catechism 1021-1022) and of the Last Judgment, which will bring to light the good each person has done (Catechism 1038-1041). The Westminster standards speak of the righteous being "openly acknowledged and acquitted" on the day of judgment (Westminster Larger Catechism 90; Confession 33). Paul himself speaks here only of praise for the faithful and does not say how these accounts fit together.

t: "Not beyond what is written": what does it mean?
p: A short saying with no verb, and a long list of explanations.
b: The Greek has just five words, to me hyper ha gegraptai, with no verb. Proposals include: (1) a reference to Scripture or to what Paul had already written (Calvin said it can be read either way, and that the choice matters little), a verse also used in debates over tradition; (2) a reference to the Old Testament passages Paul has just quoted in 1:19, 1:31, 2:9, 2:16 and 3:19-20; (3) a copy-book saying that a pupil must not go beyond the written lines; (4) a Corinthian slogan; (5) a later note that crept into the text, a conjecture some scholars have made. The phrase does not say which writings count as Scripture, and Paul praises the teaching he handed on (see 11:2; 2 Thessalonians 2:15). For a study of the verse, see M. D. Hooker, "Beyond the Things Which Are Written," New Testament Studies 10 (1963-64). "Applied" (metaschematizo) means that Paul has recast the quarrel in terms of himself and Apollos so as not to name the real leaders.

a: What do you have that you did not receive?
p: A line about grace that shaped the Western church.
b: Everything the Corinthians boast of is a gift. Augustine used this verse against the Pelagians, as Calvin notes in his commentary on 4:7: even faith is received, so no one can boast of it. Pelagius' followers answered that God gives the ability and humans choose. Catholic, Lutheran and Reformed churches follow Augustine in saying grace comes first, with different accounts of free will; Arminian and Wesleyan teaching holds that grace is given to all and can be resisted. The verse itself is aimed at pride in teachers.

a: You have begun to reign without us!
t: Irony about a kingdom that has already come
p: The Corinthians seem to think they already share Christ's rule.
b: Paul speaks with irony: "full", "rich", "kings". Some in Corinth seem to believe that the future had already arrived in the Spirit, so that they were already wise, rich and reigning. This "over-realized" view of the end fits the later denial of resurrection (15:12). The Stoics and Cynics said the wise man is a king (Epictetus, Discourses 3.22), and Paul may be teasing them with that boast. His own life, "on show last of all" (4:9), is the opposite: the kingdom is present in weakness until Christ returns.

p: Paul sees himself led out last, to die.
b: Theatron can be the theater or arena. "Last of all" and "sentenced to death" recall the end of a show where condemned men were brought out to die for the crowd (Seneca, Letters 7.3-5, describes such a midday show). Others see a Roman triumph, with captives led last in the procession (compare 2 Corinthians 2:14). Either way the apostles are not the Corinthians' glorious masters; they are condemned prisoners. "Angels" are watching too, as in the Jewish picture of the heavenly court.

a: We are fools because of Christ
p: A phrase later taken as a calling.
b: The Orthodox church honors a line of "fools for Christ's sake" (Greek saloi, Russian yurodivye), beginning with Symeon of Emesa in the sixth century, who acted foolishly to shame pride and hide his holiness. Paul's own point is sharper: the apostles' weakness and shame are the shape of the cross. L. L. Welborn reads Paul as playing the role of the "fool" of Greek comedy and mime, who tells the truth to those who think they are wise.

a: we have poor clothes, we are beaten with fists
p: Lists of hardships were a known form; Paul gives it his own use.
b: Stoic teachers listed hardships (peristaseis) to show that the wise person is unshaken: hunger, cold, blows, exile. John Fitzgerald showed the pattern, and Paul uses it here and in 2 Corinthians 4:8-9; 6:4-10; 11:23-33. The difference is that for Paul the hardships show not self-mastery but dependence on God: power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9-10). "Beaten with fists" is the verb used for the blows given Jesus (Mark 14:65).

p: Educated people looked down on this work.
b: Paul was a tentmaker or leatherworker, a trade he shared with Aquila and Priscilla in Corinth: "Their craft was making tents" (Acts 18:3). Ronald Hock argued that Paul chose tentmaking on purpose, so that no one could say he preached for gain, and that the workshop was also a place where he met and taught people. He declined Corinthian money (9:12-18; 2 Corinthians 11:7-9), which may have offended patrons who expected to support their teacher and own him. The refusal may have been another reason for the quarrel.

p: Paul may be recalling what Jesus said, without quoting.
b: Jesus taught: "Bless the ones who curse you. Pray for the ones who abuse you" (Luke 6:28). Paul gives nearly the same command in Romans 12:14. Many scholars hold that Paul knew sayings of Jesus and used them without saying so. Here he claims to do what Jesus taught, and so offers himself as the model he asks the Corinthians to copy (4:16).

a: the scum of the world, the garbage of everything
t: Two words for what is wiped away
p: Perikatharma and peripsema mean what is scrubbed off and thrown out.
b: Both words name dirt removed by cleaning. Some scholars note that in Greek cities in a crisis a person of no account might be cast out as a "purification", a scapegoat. That may lie behind these words, but the evidence is thin and later; the plain sense, "dirt we scrape off", is enough. Paul describes how the world treats the apostles, not how God does.

p: A paidagogos was a slave who supervised a boy.
b: A paidagogos walked a child to school, kept him in line and taught him manners, but was not his father. Paul says the Corinthians have many such minders but only one father in the faith, himself. He uses the picture of the Law in Galatians 3:24. "Father" language also grew into the title "Father" for priests and elders: Catholic and Orthodox churches use it and cite verses like this, while many Baptist and evangelical churches avoid the title, citing Jesus' words: "Do not call anyone on earth your 'father,' either" (Matthew 23:9). Paul uses "father" of himself only for the one who first brought them the gospel.

t: "Ways": a Jewish word for a whole life
p: Paul's "ways" are what we would call his teaching on conduct.
b: "Ways" (hodoi) is the Greek that renders the Hebrew derekh, "way" in the sense of a pattern of life and practice. Later Jewish halakhah ("walking") comes from the related verb halakh, "to walk", and names the same idea. Paul says he teaches the same ways in every church (also 7:17; 11:16; 14:33). Timothy will remind them. Paul, a Pharisee by training (Philippians 3:5), speaks as a teacher who hands on a way of life, not as a thinker with a private system. Timothy, son of a Jewish mother and Greek father, shared that world (Acts 16:1-3).

a: the kingdom of God is not in talk but in power
p: Paul uses "kingdom of God" as a present power in the church.
b: Paul speaks of the kingdom of God as a power at work now. In Romans he says, "The kingdom of God is not food and drink. It is righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit" (Romans 14:17). Elsewhere in this letter the kingdom is also a future inheritance (6:9-10; 15:50). Jesus' own sayings have the same pair, present and coming (Mark 1:15; 9:1). Here "power" means changed lives and not clever speech, the test Paul will apply when he comes.

p: A threat of discipline, offered with a choice.
b: The rhabdos is the stick of a father or teacher (Proverbs 13:24; Psalm 2:9). Paul's closing question goes with his picture of himself as father (4:15): he would rather come in love and a gentle spirit. The word "rod" does not come back, but the case of discipline at 5:3-5 shows what coming with a rod might mean, and in 2 Corinthians 13:1-2 he warns that he will not spare them if he must come.
